summary:
BlackBox72 is a bilingual educational web app that turns Ingenuity’s final flight into an interactive investigation. Students explore NASA’s 72-flight record, experiment with visual references in mission images, and build an evidence-supported explanation of the helicopter’s final landing.

A simplified visual laboratory demonstrates how removing image detail affects feature detection and matching. An evidence desk helps users distinguish documented observations from probable explanations, while a final assessment and downloadable case file support reflection.

The project addresses the challenge of preserving the stories and educational value of space hardware that remains beyond Earth. Ingenuity’s mission ended, but its achievements and limitations can still teach scientific reasoning, autonomous navigation, and responsible interpretation of evidence.

BlackBox72 uses NASA data, photographs, and published investigation findings. Its image experiment is clearly labeled as synthetic, and its educational effectiveness remains to be evaluated with students.
details:
BlackBox72 is an interactive investigation of Ingenuity’s final flight, designed for students ages 12 and up. It preserves the educational value of a spacecraft that remains on Mars by connecting its achievements, final landing, and lessons for future exploration.

HOW IT WORKS

The experience includes a visual laboratory, a flight archive, an evidence desk, and a final argument-building activity.

In the laboratory, users compare a NASA photograph with an artificially shifted copy. A simplified algorithm detects visual features and matches small image patches. Users can remove detail from the same scene and observe how the available references change. This controlled experiment illustrates a navigation concept without claiming to reproduce Ingenuity’s flight software or reconstruct its actual telemetry.

The flight archive contains all 72 flights from NASA’s published flight log. Users compare distance, altitude, speed, and duration, consult the original PDF, and download the records as CSV.

The evidence desk presents six sourced items concerning navigation, terrain, observed damage, and uncertainty. Users select evidence and develop a conclusion. Feedback emphasizes the difference between a probable explanation and a sequence proven with absolute certainty.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The app encourages students to connect claims with evidence, understand the role of visual information in navigation, and recognize the limits of available data. Spanish and English interfaces make the experience accessible to a wider audience.

Initial and final assessments support reflection, and users can download their investigation file. These assessments repeat questions, so score changes may reflect familiarity. We have not yet established educational effectiveness through testing with students.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The app uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas image processing, and browser localStorage. It runs without a backend or external runtime libraries. Progress remains in the user’s browser. NASA photographs, flight records, and published investigation findings provide the factual foundation. ChatGPT/Codex assisted development, design, writing, and translation.

CREATIVE APPROACH AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

BlackBox72 combines experimentation, data exploration, and evidence-based storytelling in one investigation. Its “black box” is a narrative metaphor; no physical flight recorder was recovered from Mars.

Design priorities included traceable sources, clear labeling of synthetic transformations, scientific uncertainty, bilingual access, and a focused demonstration that can be completed in a short session. The next step is classroom testing to assess comprehension, usability, and accessibility.
